bib.title: Investigating the Role of Prompting and External Tools in Hallucination Rates of Large Language Models

question: How do black-box prompting strategies and tool-calling agents affect accuracy and hallucination rate of a small open LLM across math, trivia and multiple-choice benchmarks?
hypothesis: The best prompting technique depends on the task type, and adding external tools may add complexity that raises hallucinations (implied by the abstract).
contributions: Empirical comparison of CoT, SC, SC-CoT, ToT, MAD, CP, CoVe, KGR, reflection and DDGA prompting at three temperatures on GSM8K, TriviaQA and MMLU
Comparison of chain and ReAct tool-calling agents against a no-tool control agent
Top-N accuracy as a signal for whether SC will help

method.summary: Prompting strategies were implemented in Python/LangChain on Llama-3-8B-Instruct Q6_K served by Ollama and run at temperature 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8, three runs each. Tool agents (chain, ReAct) used Llama-3.1-8B with Wikipedia, DuckDuckGo and Riza Python tools at temp 0.5 and were compared with a no-tool control.
method.task: hallucination mitigation via prompting and agents on math word problems, trivia QA, multiple-choice QA

datasets.name: Wikidata KG
datasets.source: used as KGR retrieval source (Vrandecic and Krotzsch 2014)

other.used_for: agents, since the Llama-3 Q6_K model does not support tool use

inference.samples: 3 runs per strategy per benchmark, means reported; SC, SC-CoT, ToT, CP use 5 samples per question
inference.prompting: Control prompt asks for answer only; CoT forces parsed reasoning steps with retries up to a tolerance (value not given); see prompts
inference.retrieval: DDGA: DuckDuckGoSearchRun snippets of user input added to prompt; KGR: Wikidata entity and property triple added to prompt

parameters.MAD: 2 debating LLMs, stop on agreement or max 10 iterations, LangChain conversation buffer; final answer from first LLM
parameters.ToT: 5 CoT samples then an LLM vote prompt (cost 6)
parameters.CoVe-2: abstain if answer without options does not match initial choice
parameters.CP: abstain when any of 5 control samples contradict
parameters.agents: chain (2 queries, bind_tools), ReAct (create_tool_calling_agent + AgentExecutor), ReAct-DDG (DuckDuckGo only, TriviaQA only); tools Wikipedia, DuckDuckGo, Riza Python sandbox

metrics.name: Hallucinated
metrics.definition: count of answers graded incorrect; abstentions are not counted (inferred from Graded + counts in Tables 2 and 3)

metrics.name: Accuracy
metrics.definition: correct over graded answers (abstained questions excluded for CP, CoVe, KGR)

metrics.name: Top-N accuracy
metrics.definition: percentage of times the correct answer appeared in N sampled answers

metrics.name: Cost
metrics.definition: average number of prompts per question

baselines: Control: base model, formatted answer only
eval.protocol: 3 runs per strategy per benchmark, means only; no statistical tests because of low power with few runs

prompts.text:
Please answer the following grade school math word problem.
The question is as follows: {question}

Please answer the following trivia question.
The question is as follows: {question}
You are a teacher grading a multiple choice exam. Generate critique and recommendations for the user's submission. Provide detailed recommendations, including the correct answer etc.
Does the answer to the verification question contradict the baseline answer?

evidence.quote: formatting instructions have been omitted for brevity

results.claim: On GSM8K, Self-Consistency at temperature 0.8 gave the best accuracy of all strategies.
results.setup: Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Q6_K via Ollama/LangChain, 3 runs averaged; GSM8K 1319 test questions; SC = majority vote over 5 samples of control prompt; baseline is control at temp 0.8
results.table: Table 1, Temperature 0.8, row SC, column Accuracy (%)

results.claim: GSM8K SC at temp 0.8 had the fewest hallucinated answers.
results.setup: Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Q6_K via Ollama/LangChain, 3 runs averaged; GSM8K; baseline control temp 0.8
results.table: Table 1, Temperature 0.8, row SC, column Hallucinated

results.claim: Explicit CoT prompting scored below the plain control prompt on GSM8K at temp 0.8.
results.setup: Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Q6_K via Ollama/LangChain, 3 runs averaged; GSM8K; CoT with parsed formatted reasoning steps
results.table: Table 1, Temperature 0.8, row CoT, column Accuracy (%)

results.claim: GSM8K SC-CoT at temp 0.5 reached 83.89% accuracy, near SC (83.80%), versus control 77.08%.
results.setup: Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Q6_K via Ollama/LangChain, 3 runs averaged; GSM8K; 5 samples
results.table: Table 1, Temperature 0.5, row SC-CoT, column Accuracy (%)

results.claim: GSM8K ToT gave only minor gains over control at temp 0.2 at cost 6 prompts.
results.setup: Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-Q6_K via Ollama/LangChain, 3 runs averaged; GSM8K; temp 0.2; ToT cost 6.00 prompts
results.table: Table 1, Temperature 0.2, row ToT, column Accuracy (%)

results.claim: On TriviaQA, Chat Protect (CP) gave the highest accuracy, 82.49% at temp 0.8, by answering only 571 of 1000 questions.

limits: Only 8B models; the authors say results for stronger models such as GPT4 are unknown
Three runs per setting, no statistical tests
Agents tested at one temperature (0.5) and on a different model (Llama-3.1-8B) than prompting strategies, so agent and DDGA comparisons are not like for like
Agents evaluated on first 1000 GSM8K questions only
Accuracy for abstaining methods (CP, CoVe, KGR) is over answered questions, so it is not comparable with control without the Correct counts
Appendix prompts omit formatting instructions; CoT retry tolerance not stated; max tokens, top_p not stated
Hallucination is operationalised as incorrect answer

terms.definition: the percentage of times that the correct answer appeared in N sampled answers
only required the formatted answer, allowing the base model to decide when to include reasoning steps
